newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian 97 budget may be rejected, deputies say.
newsitem.headline: Russian 97 budget may be rejected, deputies say.

text.p: Russia's draft 1997 budget, caught between communist and government formulas for economic growth, may well be shot down on the floor of parliament next week because deputies will not accept a compromise.
"In this shape, there is not much chance," of passing the plan, Alexei Golovkov, deputy chairman of the Duma (lower house) budget committee, said on Thursday.
Representatives of the Duma, the Federation Council upper house of parliament and the government agreed a draft budget by a razor thin margin in a reconciliation commission on Wednesday.
But deputies on both sides of the economic reform divide said this did not mean the budget would be approved when the Duma, dominated by the communist opposition, begins debating it on November 22.
Many deputies are desperate to push the shrinking Russian economy towards growth and many think it may be riskier to support a poor compromise than put a budget decision on hold.

The Duma initially rejected a government draft budget last month which called for a deficit of 91 trillion roubles ($17 billion), or 3.3 percent of gross domestic product, against the amended plan's projected deficit of 95 trillion roubles, or 3.5 percent of GDP.

But the poor record of the 1996 budget, dogged by disastrously low tax collection which has forced widespread delays in paying wages and slashed spending on investment and social programmes, has undermined the credibility of the government's plans for next year.
"If the budget is not approved at all for 1997, it will not be a tragedy," Duma speaker Gennady Seleznyov, a member of the communist faction, told a news conference on Thursday.

If the Duma fails to pass the law by year's end, which now looks increasingly likely, the government will follow the spending patterns of the 1996 budget or subsist on quarterly budgets until a law covering the full year is passed.

Golovkov said a return to such an ad hoc approach would be disastrous for the economy as local governments and firms would be hard put to plan their own fiscal years without knowing the federal government's plans.

Russia's economy presents a patchy picture -- one fifth of Russians get less than subsistence income, industrial production is half pre-reform levels, and wage arrears are rising steadily, to 35.2 trillion roubles on October 28.
On the other hand, once-astronomic inflation fell to around 27 percent, its lowest year-on-year rise, in October.

But Golovkov said Russian gross domestic product, which shrank six percent in the year to October, could grow only after the government cut its deficit, indirectly leading investors to move funds from government securities to industry.
Treasury bills, used to support the debt, offer lucrative returns that investors will not abandon until rates fall, government supporters say.
Yields on six-month treasury bills are slightly above 50 percent, and would-be borrowers face commercial bank interest rates of about 80 percent.
"The battle in the commission was over the level of internal debt," said Golovkov.
Communists, who want higher government spending to boost growth and improve social welfare, want a higher deficit.
But Andrei Illarionov, a former government economist who quit the administration in 1994 over what he called the slow pace of reform, chastised both sides for failing to slash spending.
"It's thought that world economic rules do not apply to Russia -- that's not true," he said.
($1 = 5,480 roubles)
